opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I think about a lot.

At Physical Intelligence, a lot of us came from research backgrounds, academia or big labs, where you're used to owning your own project end to end. You pick a question, you run with it, and you have a lot of freedom in how you spend your time. We've tried to keep a good amount of that. People here have real latitude to follow an idea they believe in. If someone thinks there's something interesting in a new data recipe or a different way to do action representation, they're encouraged to go try it, build a quick prototype, and show results rather than write a long proposal first.

But robotics forces you into teamwork in a way pure ML research sometimes doesn't. You can't just sit with a GPU and a dataset. You need the hardware working, the data collection pipeline running, people operating robots, infrastructure for training at scale, and evaluation on real tasks in the real world. No single person can carry all of that. So the individual freedom only matters if it plugs into a shared system that everyone is building together.

The way I'd describe the balance: individuals have freedom in *exploration*, but we're quite unified on *direction*. There's a fairly shared belief about what we're going for, general-purpose robot foundation models, and a shared stack that everyone contributes to. When a small exploration shows promise, it gets pulled into the main effort pretty quickly, and then it becomes a team thing. The person who started it doesn't own it in a territorial way anymore.

Culturally, what makes that work is low ego and a lot of trust. People are willing to drop their own idea when the evidence points elsewhere, and willing to do the unglamorous work, debugging a robot, cleaning data, fixing infra, because they know that's what actually moves the whole thing forward. Small team size helps too. When the team is small, you can see how your piece connects to everyone else's, so flexibility doesn't turn into fragmentation.

So I wouldn't say it's a tradeoff we've perfectly solved, but the goal is: give people room to be creative, and make sure that creativity flows back into one shared mission.

r001.rationale: The response describes individual latitude to choose how to explore ideas and spend time, alongside robotics work that requires people to coordinate around shared infrastructure, direction, and team efforts.

fable-5.1.text:
Kay Ke: That's actually something I think about a lot, because Physical Intelligence is a pretty unusual place in that respect. On paper it looks like a very flat, very free-form organization. There's almost no formal hierarchy, nobody is telling you "this week you must work on this task," and people have a lot of latitude to pick what they find interesting. If you want to go spend two weeks digging into some weird failure mode in the data pipeline, you can just do that.

But I think it would be a mistake to read that as "everyone does their own thing." The reason the flexibility works is that there's a very strong shared goal, which is basically: make the robot actually do the thing in the real world. That goal is extremely concrete. Either the robot folds the laundry or it doesn't. And when the goal is that concrete, it kind of self-organizes people. You don't need a manager to tell you to collaborate, because you very quickly discover that your model is only as good as the data someone else collected, and their data collection is only as useful as the policy you trained, and the policy only matters if the hardware team got the gripper to stop slipping. So the teamwork isn't imposed, it's forced on you by the physics.

The other thing I'd say is that robotics is just much more physical than, say, working on an LLM. You can't do everything from your laptop. There are robots in the office, there are people teleoperating all day, there are failures that only show up when you're standing next to the arm. So a lot of collaboration happens very naturally, very in-person, in a way that's almost old-fashioned. Someone walks over and says "hey, come look at this, it does something weird when the shirt is inside out." That kind of thing happens constantly.

So I'd describe it as: high individual freedom in how you work, but very low freedom in what you ultimately have to deliver together. And I think people who thrive there are the ones who like that combination. If you want someone to hand you a well-defined ticket every morning, it's not a great fit. If you want total independence with no accountability to the group, it's also not a great fit. It's for people who want to be trusted, but who also genuinely care whether the whole system works, not just their piece of it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts freedom in how people work and choose tasks with a shared obligation to deliver a working robot through collaboration across data, policy, and hardware teams.

astra-6.text:
I think flexibility and teamwork reinforce each other when people have a clear shared goal. You want individuals to have room to explore an idea, follow their intuition, and take ownership. But you also need people to bring what they’re learning back to the team, especially when their decisions affect someone else’s work.

In physical intelligence, that matters because the pieces are so interconnected—the model, the data, and what actually happens on the robot. So I’d aim for autonomy in how people approach a problem, with close collaboration around how those pieces fit together. The balance isn’t everyone working the same way; it’s everyone being able to move forward together.

r001.rationale: The response says people can choose how to approach a problem while collaborating closely to connect their work and move forward together at Physical Intelligence.

sol-6.1.text: I think the balance comes from giving people flexibility in how they work while staying closely aligned on what we’re trying to achieve. In robotics, that matters because the work is so interconnected—progress on models depends on data, hardware, and experiments coming together. You need room for individual exploration, but also regular opportunities to share results, surface problems, and help each other. To me, flexibility works best when it comes with a strong sense of responsibility to the team.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts flexibility in how people work and explore individually with staying aligned, sharing results, and helping each other on interconnected team efforts.
